title: Learning objectives vs learning outcomes: what is the difference?
description: Objectives describe what a session sets out to teach; outcomes state what the learner can do at the end. How they differ and which to use for compliance.
shortAnswer: A learning objective describes what a lesson or course sets out to achieve, written from the designer's point of view to plan teaching. A learning outcome states what the learner knows, understands, and is able to do on completion, written so it can be assessed. Objectives guide design; outcomes define the evidence. In regulated training, the outcome is the statement that assessment, records, and audits should rely on.
keyTakeaways: Objectives describe the intent of teaching; outcomes describe the result in the learner that must be demonstrated.
The European Qualifications Framework defines learning outcomes in terms of knowledge, skills, and responsibility and autonomy.
Public health training guidance, such as the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) guidance, uses measurable objectives with audience, behavior, condition, and degree.
The labels are used inconsistently. What matters is that the statement is observable, measurable, and tied to assessment.
For compliance and competence decisions, write outcomes first, then derive session objectives from them.

sections.heading: What is the difference between a learning objective and a learning outcome?

blocks.text: The difference is perspective and purpose: a learning objective states what the teaching intends to cover or achieve, while a learning outcome states what the learner will be able to demonstrate once the learning is complete. An objective is a planning tool for the designer. An outcome is a commitment about the learner that assessment must confirm.

In practice the two often look similar, because good objectives are also written with action verbs. The test is what the statement is used for. If it drives the choice of content and activities in one session, it is functioning as an objective. If it defines what a person must show before they are signed off, it is functioning as a [learning outcome](/glossary/learning-outcomes).

sections.heading: How do official sources define each term?

blocks.text: Official sources define outcomes by the learner's end state and objectives by what a session will deliver. The Council Recommendation on the European Qualifications Framework (EQF) defines learning outcomes as "statements regarding what a learner knows, understands and is able to do on completion of a learning process, defined in terms of knowledge, skills and responsibility and autonomy" ([Council of the European Union, 2017](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32017H0615(01))).

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), in its training design guidance, describes learning objectives as "brief statements that describe the knowledge, skills, or attitudes learners will gain by completing a lesson, course, or training session" ([CDC](https://cdc.gov/training-development/php/about/design-training-learning-objectives.html)). The same guidance separates broad training goals from objectives: goals "set the destination, but objectives map the steps to get there".

The CDC guidance recommends SMART objectives (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time bound) and the ABCD method: Audience, Behavior described with an action verb, Condition, and Degree of competency. Its example reads: "By the end of the session, nursing students will demonstrate correct handwashing technique using the CDC's hand hygiene guidelines after a simulated patient interaction, with 100% adherence." That statement already behaves like an outcome, which shows how far the terms overlap in practice.

sections.heading: Which term should a regulated organization use?

blocks.text: Use learning outcomes as the controlling statements for any training that leads to a compliance, competence, or authorization decision, and use objectives only to plan how each session builds toward those outcomes. Regulators, accreditors, and auditors ask what people can do, so the outcome is the statement your evidence must answer.

Qualification systems in many markets are built on outcomes. The EQF Recommendation asks member states to base their national qualifications frameworks on the learning outcomes approach. Workplace programs that align to those frameworks, or to a [competency framework](/glossary/competency-framework), inherit the same logic: the outcome describes performance, and the [assessment blueprint](/glossary/assessment-blueprint) shows how each outcome will be proven.

Do not spend effort policing the labels. Many organizations call everything an objective, and that is acceptable if each statement is observable and measurable and is traced to an assessment. A related source of confusion is the difference between a competence and a competency; see [competence vs competency](/compare/competence-vs-competency).

sections.heading: How does one goal break down into outcomes, objectives, and evidence?

blocks.text: One goal typically produces one or a few outcomes, and each outcome is reached through several session objectives. The example below is illustrative, for a hypothetical course on handling customer complaints in a financial services firm.

sections.heading: What mistakes happen when objectives and outcomes are confused?

blocks.text: The most common mistake is assessing the objective instead of the outcome, which produces evidence that people attended an activity rather than evidence that they can perform. Other recurring faults follow from the same confusion.

items: **Outcomes written as topics.** "Understand anti-bribery policy" names content, not performance. Rewrite it with an observable verb and a condition.
**Objectives that never reach the outcome.** Each session meets its objectives, but no activity practices the full task the outcome requires.
**Quiz items aligned to objectives only.** Recall questions about session content are used as the final assessment, so the record overstates what was proven.

**Different outcomes for the same role.** Separate courses describe the same requirement in different words, which makes [constructive alignment](/glossary/constructive-alignment) and audit mapping harder.
**No version link.** Outcomes that depend on a policy or procedure do not name the version, so they silently drift when the source changes.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry records learning outcomes in the knowledge framework before any content is written, links each to the concepts and obligations it depends on, and attaches assessment points to the outcome rather than to individual sessions. Session objectives can then be generated or written against a fixed target, and reviewers can see which outcome each piece of content serves.

faqs.q: Are learning objectives and learning outcomes the same thing?
faqs.a: They overlap but are not the same. An objective states what teaching sets out to achieve and is used to plan a session. An outcome states what the learner can demonstrate at the end and is used to design assessment. Many organizations use the words interchangeably, which is workable if every statement is measurable and linked to evidence.

faqs.q: Should a course list objectives, outcomes, or both?
faqs.a: List outcomes in the course specification and on the learner record, because those are what assessment proves. Use objectives in lesson plans and storyboards to break each outcome into teachable steps. Learners benefit from seeing both: the outcome tells them what they will be assessed on, and objectives show progress through the course.

faqs.q: Do SMART objectives count as learning outcomes?
faqs.a: A SMART objective that names the learner, an observable behavior, a condition, and a standard can serve as an outcome if it describes the end state and is assessed summatively. The label matters less than its use. If it only guides one activity and is never assessed, it remains an objective.

faqs.q: What is a training goal compared with an outcome?
faqs.a: A goal is a broad statement of purpose, such as improving complaint handling. It is not directly measurable. Outcomes translate the goal into specific capabilities that can be assessed, and objectives break those outcomes into steps for teaching.
